I’ve been working this land for 25 years, and I know what these 50 mu can handle. My well gives decent water, but the groundwater isn’t what it used to be, so I count every irrigation. Cotton has always been my backbone crop—reliable, and the buyers in Quzhou know me—so I’m putting 35 mu into cotton this year. I’ll plant a hybrid Bt cotton variety because the bollworms would eat me alive otherwise, and I’ve learned that hybrid vigor pays off on this soil. I’ll rotary till in late April, lay down base fertilizer before planting, and top-dress nitrogen when the first flowers show. Cotton is hungry, so I’ll use 20 kg of nitrogen, 8 kg of phosphorus, and 8 kg of potassium per mu. I’ll irrigate four times—at planting, early flowering, peak boll setting, and once in August if the drought bites. Four pesticide sprays are non-negotiable; I’ve seen too many neighbors lose half their yield by skipping one round.

The remaining 15 mu I’ll keep in stevia. The herb company renewed my contract, and the price per kilo is better than cotton, but the leaves are finicky. I’ll plant improved stevia seedlings in mid-May after the soil warms. Stevia needs less nitrogen than cotton—too much makes the leaves bitter—so I’ll go with 12 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu, all with rotary tillage. Three irrigations are enough if I time them right: establishment, mid-summer growth, and before the first harvest. Three pesticide applications for leaf spot and aphids should keep the stand clean. I expect 300 kg of seed cotton per mu and about 200 kg of dried stevia leaves per mu if the weather cooperates. My household only has three pairs of hands, so I keep the management simple and stick to what I know works.
